## What you can use these packages for

- **Align taxon names to any taxonomic reference you choose** -- correcting misspellings, updating
  synonyms to the currently accepted name, and matching names only identified to genus, family or any
  other rank. *(taxonAlign)*
- **Generate a taxonomic reference list for any taxon group, from any region** -- for example, as the
  taxonomic reference for a [traits.build](https://github.com/traitecoevo/traits.build) database -- from
  GBIF, the Catalogue of Life, the World Checklist of Vascular Plants, or your own table.
  *([taxonAlign.dataprep](https://github.com/traitecoevo/taxonalign-dataprep))*
- **Work directly with Australia's National Species Lists** for animals, fungi, vascular plants,
  bryophytes, lichens and algae -- both packages are designed around them. The animal, fungi,
  bryophyte, lichen and algae lists are published as dated, ready-to-use reference lists; vascular
  plants come from the Australian Plant Census. *(both)*

## Two packages

The work is split between two packages:

- **[taxonAlign](https://github.com/traitecoevo/taxonAlign)** aligns names and updates them to the
  currently accepted name. It also downloads the ready-made reference lists (the National Species
  Lists, and GBIF's list of Australian animals) from dated data releases. If your taxa are covered by
  one of those lists, or you already have a reference table in taxonAlign's format, it's all you need.
- **[taxonAlign.dataprep](https://github.com/traitecoevo/taxonalign-dataprep)** builds reference
  lists -- from GBIF, the Catalogue of Life, the World Checklist of Vascular Plants, the Australian
  Plant Census, or your own table -- and builds taxonAlign's data releases.

## Installation

Neither package is on CRAN. To align and update names, install taxonAlign:

``` r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("traitecoevo/taxonAlign")
```

To build your own reference lists as well, install taxonAlign.dataprep, which installs taxonAlign
along with it:

``` r
pak::pak("traitecoevo/taxonalign-dataprep")
```

## About this package

`taxonAlign` helps you:

1. **Fuzzy-match a list of raw taxon names** against a taxonomic reference, resolving misspellings,
   synonyms, and names only identifiable to a higher rank (`genus sp.`), to maximise how many of
   your names align successfully.
2. **Update outdated names to the currently accepted/valid name**, as long as the taxonomic reference
   you are using includes synonyms and specifies the taxonomic status of all names.

The reference can be one or more of the dated reference lists taxonAlign publishes -- the Australian
National Species List lists (animals from the Australian Faunal Directory, algae, bryophytes, fungi,
lichens) and a GBIF list of Australian animals -- your own table, or any mix of these.

It's inspired by [APCalign](https://traitecoevo.github.io/APCalign/)'s approach to aligning taxon
names to the Australian Plant Census, generalised so the reference doesn't have to be APC/APNI and
the taxa don't have to be plants and names of any taxonomic rank present in your reference (species, genus,
family, or anything else) can be matched.

## Workflow

| Function | What it does |
|---|---|
| `load_taxonomic_resources()` | Load one or more released reference lists -- `"NSL_animals"` (the Australian Faunal Directory), `"NSL_algae"`, `"NSL_bryophytes"`, `"NSL_fungi"`, `"NSL_lichens"`, `"GBIF_AU"` -- from a dated data release (downloaded once, then kept on your computer). |
| `data_release_versions()`, `data_release_datasets()` | List the available data releases, and the datasets in one; name a release with `version =` to make an alignment reproducible. |
| `taxonomic_reference_schema()`, `check_taxonomic_reference()` | The format a reference table needs to be in, and a check that a table is in it. |
| `prepare_taxonomic_resources()` | Combine one or more reference tables (released, your own, or any mix) into the structure the matching functions work on. |
| `align_taxa()` | Match a list of raw taxon names against a reference, via exact and fuzzy matching. |
| `update_taxa()` | Resolve a matched (possibly synonymous) name forward to its current accepted name. |
| `create_taxonomic_update_lookup()` | Run `align_taxa()` and `update_taxa()` together in one call -- the easiest way to go from raw names to a lookup table of accepted names. |

## Example

For Australian taxa, load one or more of the released reference lists. Each is downloaded the first
time and stored on your computer, so after that it works offline; naming the release (`version`)
makes an alignment reproducible. When a name appears in more than one list, the first listed wins:

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(taxonAlign)

animals <- load_taxonomic_resources(c("NSL_animals", "GBIF_AU"), version = "2026-10-07")
create_taxonomic_update_lookup(c("Pardalotus striatus", "Cynthia cardui"), animals)
```

Any table in taxonAlign's reference format works the same way. Here's a tiny one for the painted lady
butterfly, *Vanessa cardui*: its current accepted name, plus the name it was long known by, in the
genus *Cynthia*:

```{r example}
library(taxonAlign)

my_reference <- tibble::tibble(
  canonical_name = c("Vanessa cardui", "Cynthia cardui"),
  scientific_name = c("Vanessa cardui (Linnaeus, 1758)", "Cynthia cardui (Linnaeus, 1758)"),
  taxon_rank = "species", taxonomic_status = c("accepted", "synonym"),
  taxonomic_dataset = "MY_LIST", genus = c("Vanessa", "Cynthia"),
  taxon_ID = c("1", "2"), accepted_name_usage_ID = c("1", "1")
)
```

`create_taxonomic_update_lookup()` then matches a list of raw names -- an already-correct name, a
historical synonym, and a misspelling -- and resolves each to its current accepted name in one call:

```{r}
create_taxonomic_update_lookup(
  c("Vanessa cardui", "Cynthia cardui", "Vanessa carduii"),
  my_reference
) |>
  dplyr::select(original_name, aligned_name, accepted_name, taxonomic_status_aligned)
```

`Cynthia cardui` updates to the current accepted name, `taxonomic_status_aligned` records that it was
a synonym, and the misspelling (`carduii`, one letter off) is corrected via fuzzy matching.

See [`vignettes/get-started.qmd`](vignettes/get-started.qmd) for a full walkthrough of every function,
including building your own reference table by hand, combining several sources, matching names of
every rank (not just species), and an end-to-end "update a list of raw field names" workflow. See
[`vignettes/development-history.qmd`](vignettes/development-history.qmd) for why this package exists
and the real, messy invertebrate names that shaped its design.
